page.title: Introduction to SpringSaLaD Modeling
page.introduction:
SpringSaLaD is a particle-based, spatially resolved, stochastic simulator. Where a rule-based model treats a molecule as a set of sites that can bind and change state, a SpringSaLaD model also gives every one of those sites a place, a size and a speed: molecules are built as spheres joined by stiff springs, they diffuse and collide in a box divided by a flat membrane, and reactions happen when two binding sites approach within a binding distance with a probability determined from the specified rate constant.
It is aimed at the middle ground between molecular dynamics and stochastic simulators where molecules and species are approximated as points in space. In SpringSaLaD, sites are typically 1 to 10 nm in diameter, standing for functional protein domains; systems may be simulated for tens to a few thousand particles with time scales of about a second. Excluded volume, tethering, and the distance between one domain from another are all represented, which is what makes it the right tool for questions like ligand-mediated receptor clustering, where the geometry of the complex may affect the system behavior.
In VCell this is an Application - see SpringSaLaD Application - built on a rule-based Physiology and solved by the Langevin solver. The same rule-based Physiology may be compared to simulation results from a deterministic or network-free Application; however, the reverse is not true: currently, not every rule-based Physiology is compatible with SpringSaLaD.
page.appearance:
Molecules, sites and links. A molecule is a collection of spherical sites joined by stiff, unbreakable springs. Each site carries:
a radius, in nm, which enforces excluded volume - two sites cannot overlap;
a diffusion rate, in um2/s;
a color, used only by the 3D Trajectory viewer;
a position within the molecule, as x, y and z in nm;
zero or more states, which is where the biochemistry lives - e.g. a kinase domain that is on or off, a binding domain with and without its ligand, a residue phosphorylated or not.
The links between sites in molecules are stiff springs. They do not break, so they describe the covalent architecture of the molecule rather than any of its chemistry: a linear chain, a branched star, a ring.
Anchors and the membrane. A molecule that sits in the membrane must carry an inert site named Anchor, whose only job is to tether the other sites to the surface. The name is reserved, and so is its single state, also called Anchor. The Anchor site can be assigned a 2D diffusion coefficient, while the other tethered sites diffuse in constrained 3D - see SpringSaLaD Species.
Reactions. A SpringSaLaD reaction is an ordinary reaction rule that VCell has recognised as one of five kinds. The kinds, and the restrictions that come with them, are described in SpringSaLaD Reactions:
Creation - a zeroth order reaction that makes a new molecule out of nothing, in uM/s.
Decay - a first order reaction that destroys a molecule, in 1/s. Creation and decay together are how a species may be fixed at a roughly constant concentration.
Transition - a first order change of a site's state, in 1/s, optionally conditional on whether that site is bound.
Allosteric - a state change at one site conditioned on the state of another site in the same molecule.
Binding - a second order reaction, in 1/uM/s, that creates a spring (i.e. bond) between two sites on different molecules. Binding reactions must be reversible (although the reverse rate may be 0); the other four must not be.
